t: An open class condition recorded side shell set-in and a buckled web frame in a ballast tank after contact damage, to be re-examined at dry dock.
f: Know the open class conditions on your hull and what monitoring is expected until repair.

t: Cargo was seeping slightly from a pressure gauge valve gland on a slop tank manifold; fixed during the inspection.
f: Check manifold valves, glands and gauges for seepage at the start of cargo operations.

t: The officer had not spotted the manifold seepage at the start of cargo operations.
f: Inspect the manifold area closely when cargo starts flowing and at regular intervals after.

t: The C/E and 2/E joined within six days of each other; the reliefs could not be staggered because of a family medical emergency.
f: Plan senior officer reliefs to be staggered and tell the office early when that cannot be met.

t: SSSCL inert gas items were ticked though IG was not in use, and a junior officer could not explain the electrical insulation check he ticked every 4 hours.
f: Mark non-applicable checklist items N/A and only tick checks you understand and have carried out.

t: A bunker analysis report used ISO 8217:2005 although the stem and sample form specified 8217:2017; neither ship nor office caught it.
f: Check the standard quoted on every fuel analysis report against the stem as soon as it arrives.

t: The company entry permit had no CO2 reading; CO2 meters were still awaited before the form would be updated.
f: Use interim CO2 testing, such as detector tubes, while new meters and forms are awaited.

t: HVPQ errors: wrong ISSC expiry date, GPS shown as not fitted, tank material and coating mixed up, and PMS listed as computerised when it was paper-based.
f: Verify HVPQ entries against certificates and equipment before each upload.

t: There was no procedure or checklist for familiarising crew assigned to specialised duties that need job-specific training.
f: Ask for a job-specific familiarisation checklist for any specialised duty you are given.

t: After a change of manager only basic safety familiarisation was done; during the interview the person ticked an engine watch familiarisation checklist and presented it as done.
f: Never fill in familiarisation records without doing the familiarisation; inspectors check.

t: Posted CSO and DPA contact details showed both the old and new managers' information, and nobody had removed the obsolete notices.
f: After any change of manager, DPA or CSO, replace all posted contact notices on board.

t: Interviewee could not find the loose lifting gear or explain the procedure, and had not prepared its inventory, test and marking records.
f: Keep a loose lifting gear register showing location, ID marking and test dates.

t: The low lube oil pressure trip on an auxiliary engine failed when tested at the inspector's request, due to a faulty pressure regulating valve; fixed before he left.
f: Test engine safety trips at PMS intervals and be ready to demonstrate them on request.

t: Interviewee was not familiar with the local functional test of the main engine oil mist detector using its optical test pieces.
f: Practise the oil mist detector function test with the test glass so you can demonstrate it.

t: Also logged as a learning gap: the oil mist detector sensor unit and its simulation test were unfamiliar to the interviewee.
f: Include oil mist detector testing in engineer familiarisation and toolbox talks.

t: The VDR had failed with a DCU connection alarm; flag and port were told and a technician was working, but class had not issued a short-term certificate.
f: When statutory equipment fails, inform flag, port and class and check certificate status is updated.

t: Navigation procedures did not require the ship's UKC calculation to be reviewed with the pilot during the Master/pilot exchange.
f: Discuss and agree the UKC calculation with the pilot during the Master/pilot exchange.

t: There was no evidence the ship's UKC calculation was discussed with the pilot as the BPG expects; the officer said it was mentioned but could not show it.
f: Record the UKC discussion on the pilot card or exchange checklist so it can be shown.

t: Interviewee could not show how to mount the SART in a lifeboat or liferaft, or explain its lanyard and telescopic pole, despite recent training.
f: Practise SART mounting: the higher it is, the longer its detection range, so use the pole.

t: Oxy-acetylene lines were disconnected before port but still held 1 bar, against the procedure to drain them to zero; the pre-arrival check missed it.
f: Bleed oxy-acetylene lines to zero after isolating cylinders and check the gauges before arrival.

t: The rubber seal on an expandable scupper plug was worn and frayed; a temporary lining was fitted and replacement seals were on order.
f: Check scupper plug seals before cargo or bunker operations and carry spares.

t: Only hydrocarbon and H2S detector tubes were on board; CO, CO2, benzene and mercaptan tubes required by the company had run out and were on order.
f: Monitor detector tube stock and expiry and reorder well before stock runs out.

t: About 250 ml of oil had collected under the emergency diesel generator; it had been overlooked on routine rounds and was cleaned up during the inspection.
f: Check under and around the emergency generator on rounds, and clean up and trace any oil.

t: No suitable equipment was on board for testing heat detectors in the fire detection system; one was only ordered on the day of the inspection.
f: Make sure you have the right tools to test every detector type in the fire detection system.

t: The cargo gear crane's five-yearly load test had fallen due; an interim class annual survey had extended it, but that extension date had also passed by the time of inspection.
f: Track lifting gear test due dates in the PMS and book the retest before any class extension expires.

t: The latest Continuous Synopsis Record did not show the registered owner's identification number.
f: Check every new CSR entry against the SOLAS XI-1/5 list of required fields as soon as it arrives.

t: The P&A Manual tank table gave stripping quantities for all cargo tanks but no stripping times for any of them.
f: Review the P&A Manual tank tables for completeness and ask the office to get missing data added and approved.

t: The 3/E held 2/E certificates of competency from two administrations, but the officers' matrix showed his competency as OOW only. Corrected during inspection.
f: Cross-check the officers' matrix against each officer's CoC and endorsement every time crew change.

t: A starboard shell plate just below the main deck was indented over about 50 x 40 cm, with a maximum depth of around 40 mm.
f: Record hull damage, report it to class and the office, and keep the survey memo and repair plan on board.

t: For an inoperative BWTS the ship held only an email acknowledgement from the flag, not a formal dispensation or exemption letter.
f: When equipment fails, obtain a formal flag dispensation letter, not just an email receipt, before the inspection.

t: The PIQ gave wrong dates for the oldest ballast tank inspection and the oldest void space inspection.
f: Verify PIQ tank and void inspection dates against the actual inspection records before submission.

t: The P&I entry certificate had a clean-cargo clause requiring the club to be told before carrying persistent oil. Crude had been carried with no evidence the club was notified.
f: Read the conditions on the P&I certificate and confirm the office notified the club before a persistent oil cargo.

t: The class status report listed open conditions: suspected wastage in a ballast tank, a corroded sewage vent pipe and no Annex VI fuel sampling point on the emergency generator.
f: Know every open class condition, its due date and the corrective action status before an inspector asks.

t: A class memorandum recorded a 50 x 40 cm, 40 mm deep indent in the starboard shell plating below the main deck.
f: Be ready to explain each class memorandum, its history and any repair or monitoring plan.

t: The posted crew matrix did not match the actual sea experience of the Master, C/E and 2/E as shown in their discharge books.
f: Recalculate matrix sea time from discharge books on joining and update the posted copy.

t: The class survey status showed a different active deadweight from the one recorded in the official logbook after the last deadweight change.
f: After any change of assigned deadweight, check that class records and ship's logs show the same figure.

t: A superintendent visit declared in the PIQ had no report on board; only the report of an earlier visit was available.
f: Keep reports for every shore visit declared in the PIQ on board, or correct the PIQ entry.

t: The interviewed officer did not know the company procedure for maintaining the coating technical file for cargo and ballast tanks.
f: Know who updates the coating technical file, when, and where the procedure sits in the SMS.

t: Re-coating of the bow after contact damage and steel repairs to two cargo tanks and ballast tanks had not been recorded in the coating technical file.
f: Enter every coating repair and steel renewal in the coating technical file as soon as the work is done.

t: Coating repairs carried out in a ballast tank had not been entered in the coating technical file.
f: After any tank coating touch-up, update the coating technical file with area, product and date.

t: The class job report for repairs at the last renewal survey was not on board, so repairs to several ballast tanks could not be verified.
f: Keep class job reports for all hull and tank repairs on board as part of the ship's survey history.

t: Hardware deficiencies found during the inspection had not been entered in the defect reporting system; the ship said they had been reported to the office by email.
f: Log every defect in the company defect reporting system, even if it has also been emailed to the office.

t: The ventilation fan for the cargo heater room on the main deck was out of service.
f: Check deck space ventilation fans on rounds and raise a defect report as soon as one fails.

t: Defects entered in the defect reporting system had not been acknowledged by the office when received, although the office later approved their closure.
f: Follow up any defect report the office has not acknowledged, and record that follow-up.

t: A photo of the port manifold had been uploaded to the inspection repository where a photo of the starboard manifold was required.
f: Check every repository photo matches the exact location and side the question asks for.

t: A leak under a purifier had been temporarily contained, but it had not been reported or recorded as a defect.
f: A temporary fix is not a closed defect: record it in the defect system the same day.

t: An offshore-side manifold valve was passing, with 6 bar showing on its gauge while the ship discharged through the same manifold on the other side. It was not in the defect register.
f: Check offshore manifold gauges during cargo operations and report any passing valve at once.

t: The visual alarm at the airlock entrance to the BWTS room on deck was defective and not recorded in the defect system.
f: Test airlock alarms on rounds and log any failure in the defect system straight away.

t: The anemometer showed no wind speed and only an intermittent direction. A new circuit board was fitted but awaited maker calibration; the defect was not in the system.
f: Log a defect even while waiting for parts or maker input, and keep it open until the fault is fixed.

t: An active alarm in the cargo control room showed a valve position mismatch on three cargo tank valves; it was not in the defect system.
f: Do not leave standing alarms in the CCR: investigate each one and log it as a defect if it is not cleared.

t: A plastic tray under a running fuel oil purifier held about 2 litres of oily water from two separate leaks. No repair or report had been made, and the leak was a fire risk.
f: Treat oil leaks in purifier rooms as fire hazards: stop the leak, report it and clean up at once.

t: The accommodation elevator malfunctioned during the inspection; it was repaired before the inspection ended.
f: Report and fix lift faults promptly and keep the maintenance records up to date.

t: The speed adjusting device of a poop deck mooring winch had a minor hydraulic leak.
f: Check winch controls for leaks on every mooring station round and raise a defect report.

t: The flag's reply on the inoperative BWTS referred to a flag technical circular, but the officer had not read it and it was not on board. The office sent it during the inspection.
f: Read and keep on board every flag circular that a dispensation or flag reply refers to.

t: Many HVPQ fields were blank or wrong; for example the IG system was entered as having 20 segregations when it had none, and fitted split-drum winches were entered as not fitted.
f: Have the Master and heads of department check the HVPQ section by section against the actual ship.

t: More than 20 HVPQ items were blank or held unrealistic data, including boiler capacity, the type of fixed firefighting system and winch hauling speed.
f: Use plans and certificates to fill HVPQ technical data; never leave fields blank or guessed.

t: The HVPQ stated split-drum winches were not fitted, although the ship had them.
f: Walk the mooring deck when checking HVPQ mooring entries so the answers match what is fitted.

t: Thirteen HVPQ entries, including mooring and survey data, were blank or wrong.
f: Check the HVPQ for blank fields before every inspection request and have the office correct them.

t: The HVPQ had missing or wrong data, including the load line certificate issue date and the editions of some publications.
f: Re-check certificate dates and publication editions in the HVPQ after each renewal or new edition.

t: HVPQ entries needed updating: years under the current owner, in-water survey dates, last annual and intermediate survey dates, current deadweight and the mooring winch diagram.
f: Update the HVPQ after every survey, change of deadweight or change of owner.

t: Several HVPQ entries, including cargo tank type and mooring fittings data, were wrong or left blank.
f: Keep a checklist of HVPQ fields that change and review them before each vetting request.

t: There was no record that the firmware and software of navigation and communication equipment had been updated in the last year.
f: Keep a log of software and firmware versions for bridge equipment and record each update.

t: The side screens of the navigation lights were painted gloss black instead of the matt black required by COLREG Annex I.
f: Paint navigation light screens matt black only; check this whenever the lights are painted.

t: The last navigational assessment report did not state the assessor's qualifications.
f: Check that each navigation audit report states the assessor's qualifications before filing it.

t: The navigational assessment report did not include the assessor's relevant sea-going experience.
f: Ask that audit reports record the assessor's sea-going background, and query any that do not.

t: The operational audit declared in the PIQ had not covered tank cleaning or bunkering operations.
f: Make sure audits declared in the PIQ cover all required operations, including tank cleaning and bunkering.

t: The audit report did not include the auditor's relevant sea-going experience.
f: Check auditor qualification and experience details are in each shore audit report kept on board.

t: A behavioural competency assessment had been done by an external assessor, but the operator's guidance on the assessment programme was not on board.
f: Keep the company's behavioural competency assessment guidance on board and know where it is.

t: An engineering behavioural competency assessment was done by remote interview only; there was no record the assessor came on board, and no proof of the assessor's training.
f: Keep evidence of how and by whom each competency assessment was done, including the assessor's training.

t: The 2/O did not know why an emergency wreck marking buoy is used instead of a cardinal or isolated danger mark, or when it is removed.
f: Revise IALA buoyage, including the emergency wreck marking buoy and when it is withdrawn.

t: The duty engineer had answered night-time UMS alarms on several dates while his hours of rest record showed him resting.
f: Record rest hours honestly, including call-outs to UMS alarms, and check them against the alarm log.

t: The ship carried only 10 drug and alcohol test sample jars for 24 crew, fewer than company procedure required for post-incident testing of everyone on board.
f: Check drug and alcohol test kit stocks against crew numbers and order more before they run short.

t: Monthly hours of rest summaries sent to the office had not been acknowledged for five months, due to a software sync fault that was fixed during the inspection.
f: Check each month that the office has acknowledged rest-hour records, and raise any sync fault at once.

t: Rest-hour summaries for five months still showed as awaiting office acknowledgement in the rest-hours software; a sync fault was fixed during the inspection.
f: Do not let rest-hour reports sit unverified; chase the office if acknowledgement is overdue.

t: The familiarisation checklist listed only watchkeepers for emergency fire pump training, so catering ratings and the fitter had none recorded. A new item had been handwritten in.
f: Make sure familiarisation on critical safety equipment covers every crew member, not only watchkeepers.

t: A superintendent had sailed on board for about a week, but his shipboard familiarisation form could not be found.
f: Complete and file a familiarisation form for every visitor or riding staff who sails on board.

t: On the poop deck a mooring line had only one full turn on the leading post before being figure-of-eighted on the bitts. Corrected when pointed out.
f: Take at least two full turns on the leading post before figure-of-eighting a line on bitts.

t: A rejoining C/E boarded straight after about 15 hours of travel, against company rules requiring joining officers to be rested and to have a 12-hour handover overlap.
f: Plan reliefs so joiners arrive rested and have the full handover period the SMS requires.

t: Repairs to the incinerator refractory and an engine room damper valve were done without the cold work permit or LOTO; one engine rating on the job was not named on the permit.
f: Raise the cold work permit and LOTO for every repair and list every person working under it.

t: The relieving and relieved C/E overlapped for only about three hours, against a company minimum of 12 hours for handover.
f: Plan crew changes so the SMS minimum handover period is met; record any approved exception.

t: The relieving and relieved Masters overlapped for only about three hours, against a company minimum of 12 hours for handover.
f: If the handover period cannot be met, get office approval in writing and record it.

t: The company familiarisation form for joining crew had no item covering the ship's smoking rules.
f: Include ship-specific smoking rules and designated smoking areas in joining familiarisation.

t: Both radar magnetrons were overdue for replacement: the maker set a 4,000-hour limit and both had run over 6,000 hours.
f: Track magnetron running hours in the PMS and order spares well before the maker's limit.

t: A mooring fitting had a D/d ratio of 12.5 against the MEG4 minimum of 15. The operator mitigated by counting 1.5 hours of line wear for every hour of use.
f: Know which fittings fall below MEG4 D/d limits and apply the company's extra line-wear allowance.

t: The interviewed officer had not followed the maker's advice on when to replace the radar magnetrons.
f: Know the maker's replacement interval for radar magnetrons and check running hours regularly.

t: The terminal did not have mooring points that allowed head and stern lines to lead at least 45 degrees towards the berth face.
f: Record poor terminal mooring layouts, assess the risk and tell the terminal and the office.

t: There was no company procedure requiring the AIS to be switched off, or its aerial isolated, alongside terminals where hydrocarbon gas may be present.
f: Follow ISGOTT on radio transmissions alongside and ask the office to add AIS guidance if it is missing.

t: The interviewed officer did not know the company procedure setting machinery space team levels for traffic density, nearby hazards and weather.
f: Know how the SMS sets watch levels for traffic, hazards and weather, and how to change them.

t: The interviewed officer did not know the VDR data retention period given in the maker's manual, and the PIQ entry for it was wrong.
f: Check the VDR manual for the data retention period and make sure the PIQ says the same.

t: The safety pin on the control lever of the forward spring mooring winch was not in place. Corrected on the spot.
f: Lock winch control levers with the safety pin whenever the winch is not being operated.

t: The officer had not signed the bunker quantity verified column of the passage plan.
f: Complete and sign every check box in the passage plan, including bunker quantity verification.

t: The company SMS had no procedure for a post-voyage review of the passage plan to capture hazards and lessons for future plans.
f: Do a short post-voyage review of each passage plan and note lessons for the next one.

t: Several cancelled NAVAREA XI warnings were still marked as plotted in the navigational warnings file.
f: Remove cancelled warnings from charts and ECDIS and mark them as cancelled in the warnings file.

t: On a dedicated crude carrier using COW, IOPP Form B was marked to say COW effectiveness had not been confirmed under Reg 33, instead of the full compliance entry.
f: Check the IOPP supplement entries match how the ship is actually equipped and operated.

t: The operator had no guidance on using the survival craft portable two-way VHF radios for non-emergency communication.
f: Know company rules on using survival craft VHFs day to day and how charge is kept for emergencies.

t: The ship used the flag's GMDSS radio log as instructed, but there was no procedure for monthly and yearly GMDSS and satcom testing and maintenance.
f: Follow a written routine for daily, weekly, monthly and annual GMDSS tests and record each one.

t: There was no company procedure for recording drill details such as safety considerations and the equipment used or demonstrated.
f: Record each drill's scenario, safety precautions and equipment used, not just its date.

t: Steam was leaking visibly from the flanges of the main steam delivery valve on the aft cargo deck while heating was in use. Fixed before the inspection ended.
f: Check heating line flanges and valves on every deck round while cargo heating is in use.

t: The scenario used for the last collision drill was not realistic enough to test the ship's emergency plan.
f: Base drill scenarios on realistic local risks and run them hands-on, not just on paper.

t: Power failure and technical breakdown drills were planned twice a year, but the last two were table-top only and did not properly test the emergency plan.
f: Run blackout drills practically, with crew going to stations, not only as table-top exercises.

t: The interviewed officer could not show where the galley exhaust and supply damper closing controls were.
f: Know the location of every fire damper and ventilation stop for the galley and accommodation.

t: The CCR alarm panel showed a cargo pump casing overheat while the local engine room reading was normal at about 32 C; the cause was still being investigated.
f: Investigate cargo pump temperature alarms at once and compare remote readings with local gauges.

t: The officer had tied a fire door open with a small piece of line between the dry store and the cold provision store.
f: Never wedge or tie fire doors open; use approved hold-back devices only.

t: The fire door between the dry store and the cold provision store was held open with a piece of line. Removed during the inspection.
f: Check fire doors on safety rounds and remove anything stopping them from closing.

t: The interviewed officer did not know which hole on the lifeboat davit winch was for lowering and which for hoisting with the manual handle.
f: Know how to use the davit winch manual handle, including the hoisting and lowering positions.

t: The markings showing which hole on the port lifeboat davit winch was for lowering and which for hoisting had been painted over. Corrected during inspection.
f: Keep LSA operating markings clear and never paint over them.

t: The port lifeboat skate rubber was cracked in two places, with cracks of 5-7 cm; recent lifeboat checks had not recorded the damage.
f: Look closely at skates, fenders and fittings during weekly lifeboat checks and record any damage.

t: Cracks of 5-7 cm were found in two places on the port lifeboat skate rubber, but recent lifeboat inspection records showed no damage.
f: Do not tick lifeboat checks without looking; record and report any damage you find.

t: Asked to assemble the rescue boat radar reflector, the officer did not fit all the plates and securing pins correctly.
f: Practise assembling the rescue boat radar reflector and other loose equipment before you need it.

t: The interviewed officer had not followed company procedures for inspecting and testing rescue boat equipment.
f: Follow the SMS rescue boat inspection checklist item by item and record each check.

t: The inflatable rescue boat's manual pump was not in the boat, and its hose could not be connected to the boat's filling point when tried.
f: Check that the rescue boat pump is in the boat and that its hose fits the filling valve.

t: The officer did not know the requirement for the lifebuoy at the pilot boarding station, and a heaving line was attached to it.
f: Know the SOLAS rules for the pilot station lifebuoy and its light, including no line attached.

t: One of the three emergency lights on the poop deck at the emergency towing instructions was not working.
f: Test emergency lighting on deck regularly and replace failed units at once.

t: The starboard slop tank pressure sensor was faulty: the CCR read -2.6 kPa while a local gauge showed the actual 10 kPa.
f: Compare remote tank pressure readings with local gauges routinely and report any mismatch.

t: Cargo samples in the sample locker were not stowed in a way that kept them in line with the posted segregation table.
f: Stow cargo samples by the posted segregation table and check the locker after each loading.

t: Annex I cargo sample bottles were stowed in compartments too wide to hold them securely at sea. Corrected during inspection.
f: Use sample locker racks sized to the bottles so they cannot move in a seaway.

t: The SMS described lockout/tagout, but LOTO equipment had not been supplied; the crew were using placards and permits instead.
f: Make sure the LOTO equipment the SMS calls for is on board, and raise a requisition if it is not.

t: The interviewed officer did not know the company requirements for hot work in the machinery space.
f: Know the hot work permit steps, gas testing and fire watch rules for the engine room.

t: The ship's emergency shutdown system could not be linked to the shore ESD system.
f: Check ESD link compatibility with each terminal before arrival and agree an alternative if needed.

t: The interviewed officer did not know how to use the explosimeter and tankscope correctly or when each should be used.
f: Know what each gas instrument measures, when to use it, and how to read it correctly.

t: Monthly calibration records for portable gas detectors did not record the span gas used, the results or which alarms were tested; the procedure did not ask for this.
f: Record span gas details, readings and alarm checks every time a gas detector is calibrated.

t: During calibration both portable multi-gas detectors read wrongly: one had faulty O2 and H2S sensors, the other faulty HC, O2 and H2S sensors.
f: Bump-test detectors before use; take any that fail out of service and replace the sensors.

t: The interviewed officer did not appreciate the risk of storing paint drums high up or the injury they could cause if they fell.
f: Store heavy drums low and secured; think about falling objects when stowing stores.

t: The emergency contact details for the current port listed a location in North Korea instead of the actual port. Corrected during inspection.
f: Update the emergency contact list for each new port before arrival.

t: The officer's safety inspections of the deck had missed a defective davit on the forecastle.
f: Physically test davits and other deck fittings during safety rounds, not just look at them.

t: The forecastle davit was seized and would not turn freely. Fixed during the inspection.
f: Grease and turn deck davits regularly so they stay free to rotate.

t: Loose cable joints on three explosion-proof lamps in the cargo sample and tank cleaning heater room had not been picked up in the monthly safety inspection.
f: Check glands and cable joints on explosion-proof fittings during safety inspections.

t: The interviewed officer and the team responsible were not aware of the risks the inspector found on the deck safety rounds.
f: Use safety rounds to look for hazards, not just to tick boxes, and discuss them with your team.

t: The officer responsible for main deck safety inspections had not identified the deficiencies the inspector found.
f: Do safety rounds slowly and thoroughly; inspectors spot what rushed rounds miss.

t: The people responsible for two separate items had missed the condition of the equipment during their checks.
f: When you check equipment, look at its actual condition and report what you find.

t: Deck safety inspections had missed a cracked handrail on the port accommodation ladder and loose lifting gear with no tags or evidence of inspection.
f: Include accommodation ladders and loose lifting gear tags in every deck safety inspection.

t: About 20-25% of the IMO symbols on the fire plans at the accommodation entrances were black or grey instead of the required red, green and yellow.
f: Replace faded fire plan copies and check that symbols show the correct IMO colours.

t: The officer had locked the entrance to the emergency headquarters; a key was found and the door was unlocked during the inspection.
f: Keep emergency headquarters and fire control spaces accessible at all times.

t: Both bridge wing decks had no anti-skid gratings or anti-skid paint, and this had not been picked up on safety rounds.
f: Check walkways and bridge wings for slip resistance and report areas that need anti-skid paint.

t: The P/V breaker sight glass was dirty, making the liquid level hard to read, and the matching nitrogen main pressure was not marked next to it.
f: Keep the P/V breaker sight glass clean and mark the level that matches main pressure.

t: A hand-spliced wire sling about 2 m long was found in the engine room lifting gear store. It was removed from service.
f: Use only certified, tagged slings and remove any hand-spliced or untagged sling from use.

t: The maintenance records looked in order, but the officer had not carried out checks at the frequency set in the PMS.
f: Do PMS jobs when they fall due and record what was actually done.

t: The deck safety inspection had missed that couplings on the fire and foam lines were painted over, stopping the joints from moving. Corrected during inspection.
f: Keep fire and foam couplings free of paint and check they can be connected easily.

t: The safety inspection had missed that all mooring winch drums had been painted, contrary to COSWP.
f: Do not paint winch drums or brake surfaces; check this during mooring deck rounds.

t: 20-litre paint drums on the fourth tier of the paint locker were not secured against falling.
f: Secure paint drums with bars or lashings and keep heavy items on the lower shelves.

t: Two valves on the steam heating inlet lines to a cargo tank on deck were badly corroded.
f: Include deck heating valves in corrosion checks and the PMS and treat rust early.

t: Two floor plate covers (200 x 300 mm) over valves in the BWTS room were missing, leaving open holes.
f: Replace floor plates after work and check for open holes during safety rounds.

t: Inspection tags on portable fire extinguishers at the forecastle and cargo manifold had not been signed for the monthly checks.
f: Sign the extinguisher tag every time you do the monthly check.

t: While discharging from the starboard manifold, the sample and drain valves on the offshore port manifold were dripping cargo continuously.
f: Check offshore manifold valves and drains during cargo operations and fix any drips at once.

t: The outboard handrail of the port accommodation ladder was cracked after being hit by the winch hoist.
f: Inspect accommodation ladder handrails after each use and report any damage straight away.

t: An emergency lamp near the ladder to the emergency generator room had about 50 ml of water inside its cover, showing a leak.
f: Check that emergency light covers are sealed and dry and replace any seals that leak.

t: The positive terminals of the GMDSS batteries were uncovered. Corrected during inspection.
f: Keep GMDSS battery terminals covered and include them in the weekly battery check.

t: The MF/HF antenna on the wheelhouse top was leaning over. Fixed during inspection.
f: Check antenna mounts and stays on monkey island rounds, especially after heavy weather.

t: The internal door to the emergency headquarters and foam room was locked, with no key nearby and no notice saying where it was.
f: If an emergency space must be locked, keep the key in a marked glass box next to the door.

t: Cable joints on all three explosion-proof lamps in the tank cleaning heater room were loose and moved easily by hand. Fixed when pointed out.
f: Check that explosion-proof fittings in gas-hazardous areas are tight and properly sealed.

t: The electric garbage compactor was tried and did not work.
f: Keep garbage handling equipment working and report failures in the defect system.

t: The wheelhouse temperature stayed at about 38 C throughout the bridge inspection because the air conditioning was not working well.
f: Report bridge air conditioning faults early; heat affects watchkeepers and electronics.

t: Low insulation alarms were set at 1 MOhm on the 220 V and 440 V systems, against the 2 MOhm and 5 MOhm the procedure required, and monthly safety checks had not noticed.
f: Check insulation alarm set points against the SMS values during monthly electrical checks.

t: The low insulation alarms on the 220 V and 440 V systems could be set no higher than 1 MOhm by design.
f: If equipment cannot meet SMS set points, report it to the office so it can be assessed formally.

t: All four oxygen and acetylene flashback arrestors were more than five years past their last renewal; a requisition for new ones had been raised.
f: Track flashback arrestor renewal dates in the PMS and order replacements before they expire.

t: The bulkhead around the cargo pump hydraulic power pack had several unsealed openings to the machinery space where pipes and cables passed through.
f: Seal bulkhead penetrations after any pipe or cable work to keep fire and gas boundaries intact.

t: Missed on safety rounds: three 200-litre drums stood directly on the steel floor of the steering gear room, and the ECR switchboard mat was not marked as rated for high voltage.
f: Stow drums on dunnage and secured; make sure switchboard mats are marked with their voltage rating.

t: The sewage plant high-level alarm did not work, although records showed it was tested every quarter. Fixed during the inspection.
f: Test alarms properly, by raising the level or simulating it, not just by ticking the record.

t: No one had recognised that the cargo oil pump shafts needed proper guarding.
f: Look for exposed rotating shafts on rounds and make sure guards are fitted and secure.

t: Engine room safety rounds had missed a leaking line in the purifier room with a bottle placed under it, and low oil level in a steering gear motor.
f: Check oil levels and look for improvised drip catchers on engine room safety rounds.

t: The monthly engine room safety inspection had missed spare parts in the scrubber room secured only with a loose wire and 8 mm rope.
f: Lash spare parts properly for heavy weather and check lashings during safety rounds.

t: Steam was leaking from a valve on the bypass line of the steam supply to the cargo pump turbines in the engine room.
f: Report steam leaks at once; repair them before they cause burns or get worse.

t: The shafts of the cargo oil pumps in the engine room were not properly guarded.
f: Fit and keep guards on all rotating shafts and couplings.

t: A fireman's outfit breathing apparatus cylinder in the steering gear room was at 260 bar instead of 300 bar. It was refilled during the inspection.
f: Check BA cylinder pressures in weekly checks and refill any below full working pressure.

t: The officer responsible for machinery space safety inspections had not identified the deficiencies the inspector found.
f: Engine room rounds should find leaks, loose stores and missing guards before an inspector does.

t: An alkaline pail in use was stored in the rack marked for acid pails in the steering gear room; safety rounds had missed it. Moved when pointed out.
f: Return chemical containers to their marked racks and keep acids and alkalis apart.

t: Lube oil was seeping around the foundation bolts of the main engine on the port side.
f: Wipe and monitor engine seepage, find its source and record it as a defect.

t: One of the two water level gauge glasses on the composite boiler was out of service.
f: Keep both boiler gauge glasses working; repair a failed one as a priority.

t: The port and starboard chain lockers were not clearly marked as enclosed spaces, although they were covered by monthly forecastle safety checks.
f: Mark every enclosed space entrance with a clear warning sign and check signs on rounds.

t: A risk assessment had identified the chain lockers as enclosed spaces, but they were not marked as such.
f: When a risk assessment names an enclosed space, put warning signs on it straight away.

t: The interviewed officer did not know the operator's procedure for maintaining lifting and rigging equipment.
f: Know the SMS rules for inspecting, tagging and maintaining lifting gear.

t: A chain block in the deck store had a rusting chain and had not been maintained.
f: Clean, grease and inspect chain blocks under the PMS and tag any that are unfit.

t: A hand-spliced wire sling about 2 m long was found among the lifting gear in the engine room store. It was taken out of service.
f: Keep the lifting gear register up to date and destroy any sling without a certificate.

t: There was no risk assessment identifying the minimum spare parts needed on board for the ship's single hose handling crane.
f: With only one hose crane, assess and carry the critical spares needed to keep it working.

t: The lifebuoy with self-igniting light at the pilot boarding area had a heaving line attached to it.
f: Do not attach lines to lifebuoys fitted with self-igniting lights.

t: The officer had not noticed on routine rounds that the accommodation ladder markings were missing.
f: Check accommodation ladders for required markings as part of routine rounds.

t: Neither accommodation ladder was marked with its operating limits (design angles and loads), and there was no way to monitor its angle.
f: Mark accommodation ladders with angle and load limits and fit an inclinometer.

t: The operator gave no guidance showing an emergency escape route from the accommodation to the shore gangway or ladder.
f: Plan and brief an emergency escape route from the accommodation to the shore access at each berth.

t: One main engine unit was overdue for overhaul: the maker's interval was 16,000 hours and it had run about 16,300. Spares were on board.
f: Plan major PMS jobs ahead so they fit port stays, and get office approval for any overrun.

t: The procedure required cargo overboard and sea suction valves to be tested before every port arrival, but the C/O was testing them only monthly.
f: Test sea and overboard valves at the frequency the SMS sets and record each test.

t: The pressure gauge on the flashback arrestor of an acetylene cylinder on deck was defective. It was replaced during the inspection.
f: Check gauges and flashback arrestors on gas welding sets before each use.

t: There were no insulating deck mats at the fire pump emergency stop switch boxes in the foam room and fire control station. Fixed before the inspector left.
f: Fit insulating mats in front of all switchboards and electrical control boxes.

t: The cargo pump power pack compartment had an exhaust fan and pipe openings that let oil mist pass outside the machinery space.
f: Keep power pack compartments sealed and check fans and openings do not spread oil mist.

t: There was no risk assessment for safe operation of the incinerator.
f: Make sure a risk assessment exists for incinerator use and is reviewed before operation.

t: A shore calibration of the oily water separator had not been recorded in the Oil Record Book.
f: Record OWS calibrations, surveys and repairs in the Oil Record Book on the day they happen.

t: The annual shore calibration of the OWS and a later internal inspection of the unit had not been recorded in the Oil Record Book.
f: Record OWS maintenance and calibration in the ORB; inspectors compare it with service reports.

t: Inspector's note only: the ship was not using alternative fuels and burned HFO and LSMGO.
f: Know which fuels the ship burns and how fuel changeovers are recorded.

t: The purifier room fire doors did not close by themselves because the room was over-pressurised by supply air. Fixed by adjusting the fans during the inspection.
f: Check fire doors self-close with ventilation running and balance fans if they do not.

t: The checklist for emergencies near the ship, such as a fire on a nearby vessel or a terminal release, did not include saving VDR data.
f: Add saving VDR data to every relevant emergency checklist and know how to do it.

t: The company enclosed space entry permit gave the benzene limit as 1 ppm, while ILO, WHO and ACGIH give 0.5 ppm.
f: Know current exposure limits for benzene and H2S and use the lower value when they differ.

t: Company enclosed space procedures gave benzene and H2S limits of 1 ppm and 5 ppm, against 0.5 ppm and 1 ppm from ILO, WHO and ACGIH.
f: Check the limits on your entry permit against current industry values and report differences.

t: The shore gangway at the berth was very steep, about 30 degrees from vertical, during discharge. The Master authorised its use with special PPE for all visitors.
f: If shore access is unsafe, assess the risk, control use and record it until it can be improved.

t: The training planner had no repeat training on pilot ladder rigging, the spectrophotometer or the defibrillator; crew also needed practice starting the emergency generator in hydraulic mode.
f: Add hands-on refreshers for rarely used safety equipment to the onboard training plan.

t: The cargo officer did not know that heated cargoes and heat-sensitive cargoes must be separated by more than one tank.
f: Check cargo heating limits and required tank separation in the cargo plan before loading.

t: There were no records of maintenance or testing of each cargo tank's isolating valve; the procedure only said it should be done when needed.
f: Put cargo tank isolating valves into the PMS with a set test interval and record each test.

t: The resuscitator was not ready for immediate use because the mask and tube were not connected to the oxygen bottle. Fixed when pointed out.
f: Keep the resuscitator fully assembled and ready, and check it in weekly inspections.

t: No automatic external defibrillator was on board; a requisition for one had been raised.
f: Know whether the ship carries an AED, where it is and how to use it.

t: The ship had no emergency defibrillator on board.
f: If an AED is expected by charterers or the SMS, chase delivery and record the shortfall.

t: The air supply hose on an SCBA linked to a chemical protective suit leaked because of a faulty O-ring, which was replaced during the inspection.
f: Leak-test SCBA sets during monthly checks and carry spare O-rings.

t: The three decontamination showers were not marked prominently enough: the stickers were small and the posts were the same colour as the deck.
f: Paint safety shower posts in a high-visibility colour and mark them so they can be found quickly.

t: The inert gas scrubber cooling sea water pump had a heavy leak from its shaft seal.
f: Check IG plant pumps for seal leaks and repair them before the IG system is needed.

t: The overfill alarm on one cargo tank had been abnormal since arrival, but the officer had taken no corrective action.
f: Never accept a faulty overfill alarm; report it, take extra precautions and get it fixed.

t: The officer could not find the company procedures for carrying inhibited cargo in the electronic SMS; a senior officer showed them later.
f: Know where to find cargo-specific procedures, such as for inhibited cargoes, in the SMS.

t: The interviewed officer was unable to locate the procedure for inhibited cargoes in the electronic SMS until a senior officer found it.
f: Before loading a special cargo, read the SMS procedure for it and know where it is.

t: The officer's monthly records showed the SCBA sets for chemical protective equipment in good order, but a faulty O-ring was found when they were tested.
f: Actually test SCBA sets during monthly checks rather than just looking at them.

t: The nitrogen room had an oxygen readout outside the starboard door but none outside the port door.
f: Fit oxygen readouts at every entrance to the nitrogen room and check them before entry.

t: One of the two toxic gas (VOC) detectors gave wrong readings.
f: Calibrate toxic gas detectors and take any that read wrongly out of service.

t: The officer did not know the operator's maintenance procedure for the IG scrubber cooling sea water pump.
f: Know the maintenance routine for IG plant equipment you are responsible for.

t: One cargo tank's 98% overfill alarm kept sounding and could not be reset although the level was below 95%, and the 95% high-level alarm did not trigger.
f: Test high-level and overfill alarms before each cargo operation and report any fault at once.

t: A static accumulator cargo melting at 13 C was being discharged with night temperatures below 10 C, but the discharge plan had no warning about either hazard.
f: Include static and solidification risks, with precautions, in the cargo plan.

t: The flag allowed treated sewage to go into a ballast tank by hose on condition the tank was locked out against ballast operations. The officer had not locked it out.
f: When the flag or company imposes a condition, carry it out and record that you did.

t: The cargo and ballast plan had not been signed by the engineers supporting cargo operations, despite concurrent bunkering, and there was no company guidance to involve them.
f: Have engineers attend the cargo meeting and sign the plan, especially when bunkering at the same time.

t: The officer had not checked that the deck air compressor driving the spill response pumps was running before the cargo hoses were connected.
f: Check spill response pumps and their air supply are ready before connecting hoses.

t: The secondary alarm monitoring system in the cargo control room showed a module failure alarm; it had been entered in the defect system.
f: Keep CCR alarm systems fault-free and know how to work around any failed module.

t: When tested, the air-driven spill response pumps would not start because the deck air compressor was off; it took about 5 minutes with hoses already connected.
f: Start the deck air compressor and test spill pumps as part of the pre-transfer checklist.

t: The officer could not produce the pre-cargo safety meeting record for the current discharge, as required by procedure.
f: Hold and record the pre-cargo safety meeting before every operation and keep it in the CCR.

t: There was no evidence that the brake test kit's pressure gauge had been calibrated or compared with a calibrated gauge before winch brake testing.
f: Check the brake test gauge's calibration certificate before each winch brake test.

t: A fire hydrant on the lower engine room platform was mounted about 6 ft up, near the emergency exit and facing a nearby bulkhead, so a hose would kink and supply could be restricted.
f: Check hydrants can be connected and the hose run without kinks, and report badly placed ones.

t: The pre-mooring toolbox meeting record just said 'risk assessment - yes', without stating which assessment was used or which risks were discussed.
f: Write down which risk assessment was used and the main hazards discussed in each toolbox talk.

t: The mooring toolbox meeting record gave no detail of the risk assessment used or the specific risks discussed with the mooring team.
f: Make toolbox records specific: name the assessment, hazards, controls and who attended.

t: The officer did not know that mooring winch operating levers must be locked.
f: Lock winch levers when not in use, with the pin or lock provided.

t: Snap-back zones were permanently painted on deck, giving a false sense of safety outside them. MEG4 treats the whole mooring area as high risk, to be marked with barriers and signs.
f: Treat the whole mooring deck as a danger zone; use barriers and signs, not painted zones.

t: The closed chocks, cruciform bollards and deck pad-eyes used for hose handling at buoy moorings were not in line with each other.
f: Report misaligned hose-handling fittings and plan hose lifts around them until fixed.

t: Class or other independent certificates for the forward bow fairleads, stopper and their supporting structure were not seen during the inspection.
f: Keep class certificates for bow fairleads, stoppers and their foundations on board.

t: The C/E's standing orders did not set out what to do when a machinery alarm sounds (especially on critical equipment), when a defect is found, or limits for hot and cold work in the workshop.
f: Make sure C/E standing orders cover alarm response, defects and workshop hot work, and read them.

t: The C/E wrote and signed engine room night orders daily but did not record the time, and the procedure did not require it.
f: Date, time and sign night orders so it is clear which instructions were in force.

t: Empty oxygen and acetylene cylinders were not kept apart from full ones in the cylinder stores.
f: Separate and mark empty and full gas cylinders in the store.

t: The bunker checklist required bunker tank atmosphere checks 24 hours before and after bunkering but none during the transfer.
f: Monitor bunker tank vapours, including H2S, during bunkering as well as before and after.

t: During the last bunkering, the designated smoking rooms were not entered in the ship-shore safety checklist.
f: Fill in every field of the bunkering safety checklist, including designated smoking areas.

t: The SMS required the C/O to measure bunker tank atmosphere daily after bunkering and pass readings to the C/E for the engine log; this was not being done.
f: Take and log daily bunker tank gas readings after bunkering as the SMS requires.

t: Indicator cocks on two running diesel generators had no insulated caps fitted; recent rounds had missed this and it took about 2 hours to fix.
f: Keep insulated caps on indicator cocks of running engines to prevent burns and fire.

t: The oil mist detector sensors had not been calibrated at the 12-monthly interval set by the maker.
f: Put maker calibration intervals for safety devices like oil mist detectors into the PMS.

t: Under the photo questions, the inspector noted that no P/V breaker was fitted because the ship had a nitrogen system installed.
f: If a fitting asked for in the photo set does not exist on board, explain why in the repository.

t: The uploaded photo did not show the forward end of the hull on the port side as required.
f: Take repository photos from the exact angle and position the question specifies.

t: The uploaded photo did not properly show the port side of the forecastle looking towards the fairleads.
f: Check each repository photo against the question's description before uploading.

t: The uploaded photo did not clearly show the winch brake setting; the inspector took and attached a new one.
f: Make sure close-up photos show the detail asked for, such as brake marks, clearly.

t: A photo of the port manifold was uploaded where a photo of the starboard manifold was required.
f: Label photos with location and side when taking them so the right one is uploaded.

t: A photo of the emergency towing arrangement stowage was uploaded under the wrong question.
f: Match each photo to its question number and double-check before submitting.

t: The uploaded photo for this question did not include the fairleads.
f: Include every item named in the question in the photo frame.

t: The uploaded photo did not show the local control station; the inspector took a new photo.
f: Retake repository photos after any change so they show the current arrangement.

t: The ship had an electrolysis-type BWTS, but chlorine was not tested before entry into ballast tanks.
f: Add chlorine to the gas test list for ballast tank entry on ships with electrolytic BWTS.

t: No photo had been uploaded to the repository for this question; the inspector attached a photo of the P/V valve rack.
f: Check the photo repository is complete before the inspection is requested.

t: The ship had no P/V breaker fitted; a nitrogen generator was used for inerting cargo tanks when needed.
f: Explain non-fitted equipment in the repository instead of uploading an unrelated photo.

t: The uploaded photo showed a single cargo tank P/V valve instead of a P/V breaker, which was not fitted.
f: Never upload a substitute photo; state clearly when the item is not fitted.

t: The uploaded photo did not show the double block and bleed valves; the inspector attached a representative photo.
f: Make sure photos of valve arrangements show every valve the question refers to.

t: The ship had submerged cargo pumps but no photo of them had been uploaded; the inspector took one.
f: Upload a photo for every question that applies to the ship's equipment.

t: SEEMP Part III did not explain how waste heat recovery, just-in-time arrival or rudder optimisation could lower the ship's carbon intensity rating, which was C.
f: Know the ship's CII rating and the measures in SEEMP Part III to improve it.

t: The repository said the ship was not classed for ice navigation, although it held an ice class notation.
f: Check the class certificate when answering ice class and other class notation questions.

t: Patches of mechanical damage and rust were seen on the boot-topping on the port side, near ballast tanks forward and aft.
f: Record hull coating damage at each port and plan touch-ups when conditions allow.

t: The emergency generator room ventilation was not clearly marked; the original marking had been partly painted over.
f: Keep ventilation openings and closures clearly marked and do not paint over the markings.

t: About 20% of the catwalk gratings were moderately rusted.
f: Include catwalk gratings in deck maintenance and treat rust before it weakens them.

t: About 30% of the catwalk gratings were moderately rusted.
f: Plan a catwalk grating maintenance programme and renew badly rusted sections.

t: The midship draught marks between 12 and 14 m were faded; crew put this down to frequent Panama Canal transits.
f: Repaint faded draught marks at the first chance and check them after canal transits.

t: One stud on a link of the port anchor cable was partly out of position.
f: Inspect anchor cable studs during anchoring and report loose or displaced ones.

t: An openable window on an accommodation deck had bars welded across it for piracy areas, so it could no longer be used as an escape route.
f: Make sure anti-piracy hardening does not block escape routes; use removable bars where needed.

t: One toilet on the upper deck needed repair to be usable.
f: Report and fix sanitary defects promptly; inspectors note accommodation upkeep.

t: The tank cleaning plan did not mention the portable cleaning machines, although they were used every time as the charterer's guidance required.
f: List every machine and method you will actually use in the tank cleaning plan.

t: During discharge the terminal regulations were not in the CCR and the junior deck officer did not know them; they had come by email and only a senior officer knew them.
f: Print terminal rules received by email, brief all cargo watch officers and keep a copy in the CCR.

t: Remote indicators in the cargo system read wrongly; for example one showed 48% when the item was fully open.
f: Compare remote indications with local positions before cargo operations and report mismatches.

t: The tank cleaning plan had no dates and no record of the toolbox meeting held.
f: Date every tank cleaning plan and record the toolbox meeting held before starting.

t: The crew were filling in an inert gas log although the ship had no IG system, only a nitrogen generator.
f: Use log forms that match the ship's actual equipment and ask the office for the right ones.

t: All mooring winches were marked with brake holding capacity, whereas the marking should show brake rendering capacity at 60% of the ship design MBL.
f: Know the difference between brake holding and rendering capacity and check winch markings.

t: Part 6 of the mooring system management plan was blank and based on 60% of line MBL, and neither the MSMP nor the line plan gave ship design MBL or line design break force.
f: Make sure the MSMP and line management plan record ship design MBL and line design break force.

t: The MSMP said nothing about turns on the split drum: maker and MEG4 call for 6, but the rope and drum allowed only 4, dropping to 2-3 during discharge.
f: Know the minimum turns needed on the tension drum and check them as the ship rises during discharge.

t: The IMO life-saving signals poster was not available or posted on the bridge.
f: Keep the SOLAS life-saving signals table posted on the bridge.

t: The engine watch level required by the company was not recorded in any logbook, including when it changed.
f: Log the engine watch level and every change to it with the time.

t: The compass deviation card prepared on board was incomplete, with no record of the corrector magnet and Flinders bar positions.
f: Record corrector magnet and Flinders bar positions on the deviation card when it is prepared.

t: No visual bearings were taken to check the ship's position on departure, although several conspicuous landmarks were available.
f: Cross-check GNSS positions with visual bearings whenever landmarks are available.

t: Cross-track limits were set at 1 nm and the route checked over that width, but standing orders required 3 nm from dangers and passing ships, so the ship often sailed in unchecked water.
f: Set the route check corridor wide enough for every deviation standing orders allow.

t: Company policy for safety contour and safety depth did not account for the lowest tidal height, even in coastal waters and tidal ports, contrary to NP232 guidance.
f: Work out safety depth and contour from actual draught, squat and the lowest expected tide.

t: There were no records of checks on the accuracy of the speed input from the Doppler log.
f: Compare log speed with GNSS speed over ground regularly and record the results.

t: The GPS HDOP alarm, set at 4 according to the manual, could not be found in any menu of the receiver.
f: Know where alarm limits like HDOP are set on each GNSS receiver and check them.

t: The list of critical bridge equipment defined in the SMS was neither posted nor available.
f: Post the critical equipment list on the bridge and know which items are on it.

t: Echo sounder depth comparisons were not done properly across the different ranges, and some past records showed differences of 2.5 m or more.
f: Compare echo sounder depths with charted depths on each range and investigate big differences.

t: The C/E's standing instructions did not cover the engine watch level.
f: Make sure the C/E's standing orders explain engine watch levels and when to change them.

t: The UMS checklist was not ship-specific and had many N/A items, and the superintendent-approved copy was not on board.
f: Use a ship-specific UMS checklist approved by the office and keep the approved copy on board.

t: There were not enough photoluminescent IMO arrow signs along the engine room escape routes and emergency exits on the various platforms.
f: Walk each engine room escape route and add direction signs wherever they are missing.

t: Many critical items were not identified or included in the spares list; for example GMDSS equipment had no spares and was not listed.
f: Check that every critical equipment item has listed minimum spares and that stock is held.

t: The main engine emergency stop had not been tested as required by SOLAS and MSC.1/Circ.1432, and there were no records of earlier tests.
f: Test main engine emergency stops at the interval MSC.1/Circ.1432 gives and record the result.

t: The X-band magnetron was listed as a critical spare but none was on board (requisition raised), and the S-band magnetron was not listed as a critical spare.
f: Keep spare magnetrons for both radars and treat them as critical spares.

t: The emergency generator on-load test duration was not recorded; an engineer said it ran about 10 minutes when it should run 30.
f: Run the emergency generator on load for the full required time and record start and stop times.

t: Over the past year none of the bunker checklists showed bunker tank vapours (H2S and benzene) being checked and recorded during bunkering.
f: Measure and record H2S and benzene in bunker tank vapours during every bunkering.

t: The cyber security plan had no ship-specific information: the annex listing the ship's IT and OT assets was not filled in.
f: Keep the ship's IT/OT asset list in the cyber plan complete and up to date.

t: The cyber security plan did not give contact details for the ship's IT manager.
f: Make sure the cyber plan names the IT contact and how to reach them in an incident.

t: Many USB and network ports were left open on operational terminals in the CCR and ECR.
f: Block or lock unused USB and network ports on operational computers.

t: The cyber security manual listed wrong computer operating systems for the ship, such as an outdated Windows version that was not in use.
f: Check the cyber manual describes the ship's actual computers and software.

t: No cyber security assessment was available on board.
f: Keep the ship's cyber security assessment on board and know its main risks.
